So, let me talk about the autoencoders. The first autoencoder that comes into picture is fully connected autoencoder, where the architecture is: encoder, latent space, decoder. What does encoder do? The encoder takes the image and flattens the image, performs encoding and generates one latent space that is the compressed form, and the latent space output is given as input to decoder, and decoder will try to reconstruct the image. The first main reason why fully connected autoencoders fail is because the 2D dimension of image is directly flattened, losing all spatial neighborhood information. Hence, with this particular drawback, we go for convolutional autoencoders where the 2D image is not flattened directly, but we perform convolution operations, pooling operations, understanding spatial features, and then give it to encoder to get latent space.

Still, what do we observe? In convolutional autoencoders, the reconstructed image has improved clarity, but it is not sharp, and when we sample from random points in the latent space, we get meaningless noise. Why do we use autoencoders? In image processing, we have huge training images, so training time becomes complex. To reduce computational complexity, we compress the image so the size of the image is reduced while preserving features.

Now, there are applications where I want to generate novel images, not just reconstruct. So the third type of autoencoders that came into picture is Variational Autoencoders, or VAEs. The reconstruction accuracy increases from 50 or 60 percent up to 80 or 90 percent. But the main idea here is: what extra thing can I do with this latent space? In normal autoencoders, the encoder outputs a single deterministic point in latent space.

When you talk about the normal encoder, you understand where exactly the single data point is. But when we talk about the variational autoencoder, we do not want to look at one fixed point where the data is available. We want to understand the probability distribution of data in the latent space. So, the improvement in the latent space is done not by a single point, but by predicting two vectors: the mean (mu) of the data distribution, and the variance (sigma squared) of the data distribution.

What is mean and what is variance? Mean is the average sample point, and variance tells how spread out the data is around the mean. So instead of a deterministic bottleneck, the encoder outputs parameters of a probability distribution! Now, how do we regularize this? We want the mean and variance to be close to a standard normal distribution, with zero mean and unit variance.

Why? If we do not regularize, the network will simply set variance to zero and push different classes infinitely far apart in latent space to make reconstruction easy. Then there would be large empty gaps in latent space where sampling produces gibberish.

To prevent this, the loss function of a VAE has two components:
First, the reconstruction loss, which measures how well the decoded image matches the input.
Second, the KL divergence—Kullback-Leibler divergence—which acts as a regularizer. The KL divergence measures the distance between the learned latent distribution and the standard Gaussian prior N(0, I). It penalizes the encoder whenever mu drifts away from 0 or sigma deviates from 1.

So the KL divergence makes sure that the latent space is smooth, continuous, and has no empty gaps! When this kind of compression is done, you can pick any random point from the latent Gaussian space, pass it to the decoder, and generate a completely realistic, novel image. Before we get into code, let us understand how the reparameterization trick allows backpropagation through this random sampling step...

Variational Autoencoders: focus on continuous latent space. Normal autoencoders map to a single deterministic point. VAE maps to a probability distribution...
Predicting Gaussian parameters: mean mu and variance sigma^2. Why KL divergence? KL divergence regularizer forces latent space close to N(0, I), preventing gaps and enabling generative sampling...
